title: Primordial Black Holes May Have Reheated Universe, but Mass Spread Makes Theory Hard to Test
excerpt: Primordial black holes may have reheated the universe, according to a Mainz physics model. A spread of black hole masses mutes the gravitational wave signal that once threatened the idea, but the authors say future detectors probably cannot test it, leaving the theory viable yet hard to confirm
content:
Microscopic black holes born just after cosmic inflation may have evaporated early enough to release the energy that turned a cold, empty cosmos into the hot plasma of the Big Bang, according to a Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz release dated Nov. 19. The result is a theoretical model, not an observation: giving the black holes a spread of masses mutes the gravitational-wave signal that once threatened the idea, but the authors say future detectors probably cannot confirm it either.

For readers who follow cosmology, the stake is specific. Because reheating has no direct observations, and this paper shows that one rival explanation survives a test that looked fatal to it, the first instants after inflation are less constrained, not more. Yann Gouttenoire of the Institut d'Astrophysique de Paris, with Nicholas Leister and Pedro Schwaller of Mainz, published the work in Physical Review Letters on Oct. 29 under the title "Reduced Gravitational Wave Signal Reopens the Ultralight Primordial Black Hole Window."

What Is Reheating After Cosmic Inflation?

Mainz places inflation, the burst of extremely rapid expansion at the start of the universe, between roughly 10⁻³⁵ and 10⁻³³ seconds after the beginning. Inflation leaves the universe in a non-thermal state, with essentially all of its energy in the inflaton field, so something must convert that cold state into the hot, dense plasma from which particles and later atoms formed.

Reheating is that conversion. In the textbook picture, the inflaton field's energy becomes a hot thermal bath of Standard Model particles, often starting with a phase of parametric resonance called preheating, followed by fragmentation and thermalization. Reheating must produce mainly Standard Model particles and reach a final temperature above 1 MeV so that Big Bang nucleosynthesis can proceed, yet its details remain unknown because no direct observations from that era exist.

That temperature floor is the deadline for the black-hole scenario. Nucleosynthesis, the period when the first light nuclei formed, began once temperatures fell below roughly 1 MeV and left the universe at about 75% hydrogen and 25% helium-4 by mass, so any reheating route has to finish before it starts. The paper therefore limits its black holes to masses below about 10⁹ grams (1,000 metric tons, about 1,100 US tons), which evaporate before nucleosynthesis.

Black Holes Come to Dominate Energy Budget Before Evaporating

In the Mainz scenario, tiny primordial black holes (PBHs) formed shortly after inflation and came to dominate the early universe. Because the lightest ones evaporate first through Hawking radiation, that evaporation heated the universe into a plasma.

Hawking radiation is the mechanism doing the work. A black hole's radiation temperature is inversely proportional to its mass, so smaller black holes run hotter, and the evaporation lifetime scales as the cube of the initial mass. A solar-mass black hole would take more than 10⁶⁷ years to evaporate, far longer than the universe's age of about 14 billion years, so only very small black holes can vanish in time. The Mainz release says the smallest primordial black holes may have been smaller than an atom. A representative case in the paper's first figure uses black holes of 10⁴ grams (10 kg, 22 lbs).

Black-hole reheating is not new. Md Riajul Haque, Essodjolo Kpatcha, Debaprasad Maity and Yann Mambrini proposed black-hole reheating in May 2023, finding two possible histories: one where the inflaton stays dominant and black holes supply the thermal bath, and one where black holes dominate and their evaporation produces a radiation-dominated universe. That paper examined extended mass distributions too. What the Mainz team adds is the gravitational-wave consequence of a realistic spread, which, in their companion paper, reopens regions of parameter space previously thought excluded.

Equal-Mass Black Holes Would Trigger Poltergeist Gravitational Waves

If every black hole had the same mass, nearly simultaneous evaporation would switch the universe abruptly from matter domination to radiation domination. Physicists call the resulting enhancement of induced gravitational waves the poltergeist mechanism; a review by Inomata, Kohri and Terada uses that name, while a 2020 preprint by Inomata and colleagues found that the enhancement depends on how long the black-hole era lasted and how broad the mass distribution is.

In that review's account, density perturbations grow during matter domination and then oscillate rapidly once pressure returns, which strongly amplifies the induced gravitational waves. A sudden switch maximizes the effect; the Mainz papers argue that a smoother transition sharply weakens it.

The consequence was a possible veto. For single-mass black holes, the Poltergeist-dominated signal can violate the nucleosynthesis limit on extra relativistic species, ΔN_eff below 0.34, which caps how much radiation-like energy gravitational waves could add during that era. That limit exists because light-element abundances depend on radiation energy density.

Critical Collapse Forces Low-Mass Tail That Smooths Reheating

The Mainz team argues the single-mass assumption is unrealistic. Niemeyer and Jedamzik proposed in 1998 that the universal scaling between black hole mass and initial perturbation seen near the threshold of collapse also applies to primordial black holes, so black holes can form with masses below the horizon mass.

For black holes forming in a radiation-dominated universe, the irreducible collapse mass tail scales roughly as M^3.78 per logarithmic mass interval, which follows from an exponent of about 0.36 derived from simulations relying solely on general relativity and spherical symmetry. Lighter black holes therefore evaporate earlier and heavier ones later, so reheating becomes gradual instead of abrupt.

The authors report that this tail suppresses the Poltergeist contribution "by orders of magnitude," though the paper gives no single suppression factor, and that the nucleosynthesis bound is entirely relaxed, which the single-mass case could violate. In the companion paper, they split the scalar-induced signal into eight production channels and find that, apart from the one tied to black hole formation, none reaches the current extra-radiation bound or the projected sensitivity of future detectors.

Hawking Radiation and Primordial Black Holes Both Remain Unobserved

The scenario stacks two unconfirmed ingredients. Hawking radiation, proposed in 1974, is predicted to be far too faint to detect from known black holes, and a 2018 search of Fermi data for nearby evaporating primordial black holes came up empty.

Primordial black holes themselves are also unconfirmed. Standard slow-roll inflation produces fluctuations too small to make them, so enough black holes to matter typically require exotic inflation models, which critics say need significant fine-tuning.

Future Gravitational-Wave Detectors Probably Cannot Test This Theory

Leister put the testing prospect bluntly: "Future gravitational wave experiments probably won't be able to probe this theory." The paper compares the predicted signal with the most optimistic combination of sensitivity curves, assuming total astrophysical foreground subtraction, across SKA, Theia, μAres, LISA, AEDGE, BBO, DECIGO, the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer.

The result carries stated limits. The mass tail assumes general relativity and spherical symmetry, the induced-wave calculation is linear, and gravitational waves from halo formation after fluctuations turn nonlinear are excluded. Discarding the high-mass end of the distribution gives the largest possible signal, so the authors treat that choice as a conservative upper limit, while their most extreme cutoff is an extrapolation and the detailed transfer functions are deferred to the companion paper.

Mainz presents the work as showing that a black-hole-dominated early universe is possible, not as a confirmed observation. The scenario becomes harder to rule out and, for now, equally hard to confirm.

Ultra-Light Black Holes Cannot Be Dark Matter, but Heavier Ones Remain Candidates

Black holes this light cannot be dark matter today. Hawking's work implies that primordial black holes below 10¹² kg (2.2 trillion lbs) would not have survived to the present, a threshold a million times the 10⁹ gram (1,000 metric tons) ceiling in this paper.

Heavier candidates remain under study. A separate Mainz analysis in Physical Review Letters, "Closing the Mass Window for Stupendously Large Black Holes," used Planck satellite data to find no sign that such objects formed shortly after the Big Bang make up a significant part of dark matter; the release is dated Nov. 6. Whether a sub-solar-mass candidate reported in November 2025 by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration is a real primordial black hole signal or noise remains disputed.

Reheating Mechanisms Now Compete Without Direct Observational Arbiter

Inflaton decay remains the textbook route, and nothing in this paper displaces it. What changes is the field of live options: black-hole evaporation now survives the gravitational-wave test that seemed to exclude it, while the same smoothing that rescues it also leaves it probably beyond detector reach. With no direct observations of the reheating era, the choice between mechanisms rests on theory and on indirect limits such as the requirement that reheating exceed 1 MeV for nucleosynthesis.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is reheating in cosmology?

It is the phase after inflation when the energy that drove rapid expansion becomes the hot, dense particle plasma at the start of the Big Bang. Its details are still unknown.

Why does a spread of black hole masses matter for reheating?

Equal-mass black holes would evaporate nearly together and produce a strong Poltergeist gravitational-wave signal that could break nucleosynthesis limits. A mass spread makes evaporation gradual, which the authors say sharply weakens that signal.

Does this prove black holes, not inflaton decay, reheated the universe?

No. The paper shows black-hole reheating is viable and harder to exclude, not that it happened, and detectors probably cannot test it.

Could these ultra-light primordial black holes be dark matter?

No. Black holes below about 10⁹ grams (1,000 metric tons) would have evaporated long before today, while heavier primordial black holes remain dark matter candidates in parts of parameter space.
